boundary_rationale: Psalm 127's title names Solomon, “A Song of Ascents. By Solomon.” (web:Ps.127.0 = oshb:Ps.127.1, שִׁ֥יר הַֽמַּֽעֲל֗וֹת לִשְׁלֹ֫מֹ֥ה, byte tier), the part's only such ascription (sweep: 12 titles, 1 li-Shlomo). Its opening verse pairs two 'unless Yahweh' clauses about futile labor, “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” (web:Ps.127.1), and web:Ps.127.2 extends the same futility to a worker's own daily toil, “It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.” This pair of verses forms a self-contained panel on labor without Yahweh's blessing, bound by the repeated שָׁ֤וְא (oshb:Ps.127.1, word indices 8 and 17) and שָׁ֤וְא (oshb:Ps.127.2, word index 0) -- three occurrences in these two verses, word-bound skeleton sweep: 10 verses book-wide -- and absent from web:Ps.127.3-web:Ps.127.5. The seam itself is marked by an addressee shift: the psalm's only second-person form, לָכֶ֨ם (oshb:Ps.127.2, byte tier), gives way at web:Ps.127.3 to the presentative הִנֵּ֤ה (oshb:Ps.127.3, byte tier; verse-initial skeleton sweep: 14 verses book-wide) with third-person description; web:Ps.127.3 turns to a new subject, children as Yahweh's own gift, without returning to the house-and-city figures, corroborating the same seam between this panel and the psalm's second panel (web:Ps.127.3-web:Ps.127.5).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Psalm 127 as one whole-psalm row was considered, since the part's short psalms default to one row, but rejected because the psalm divides at an addressee shift: the second-person לָכֶ֨ם of web:Ps.127.2 (oshb:Ps.127.2, byte tier) -- the psalm's only second-person form -- gives way to the presentative הִנֵּ֤ה of web:Ps.127.3 (oshb:Ps.127.3, byte tier) with third-person description, while the repeated שָׁ֤וְא that binds web:Ps.127.1-web:Ps.127.2 (three occurrences, word-bound skeleton sweep: 10 verses book-wide) is absent from web:Ps.127.3-web:Ps.127.5; the psalm's topic change from futile labor to Yahweh's gift of children corroborates the same seam.

boundary_rationale: “עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֑ב” (oshb:Ps.135.15) -- “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.” (web:Ps.135.15) -- opens an idol polemic that runs through mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see (web:Ps.135.16), ears that cannot hear (web:Ps.135.17), to the closing verdict, “Those who make them will be like them, yes, everyone who trusts in them.” (web:Ps.135.18). This four-verse unit shows cross-psalm texture with Ps 115's idol polemic (115:4-115:8): a word-by-word byte comparison of both psalms' own text (verse_map_oshb.json) finds oshb:Ps.135.16 matching oshb:Ps.115.5 and oshb:Ps.135.18 matching oshb:Ps.115.8 letter-for-letter, while 135:15's construct chain with the article (עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם) differs from 115:4's suffixed plural (oshb:Ps.115.4: עֲֽ֭צַבֵּיהֶם), and אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ אַ֝֗ף אֵין יֶשׁ ר֥וּחַ בְּפִיהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.135.17) as a whole verse runs longer than 115:6 alone on all 3 measures taken (9 vs 8 skeleton words, 32 vs 30 consonants, 70 vs 67 codepoints), shorter only against 115:6-115:7 combined (17 skeleton words / 70 consonants / 156 codepoints with one joining space), and its clause shared with 115:6, אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ, substitutes a different verb root (יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ for oshb:Ps.115.6's יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ) inside the four words the two verses hold in common. It is discussed here as a recognizable, recurring cross-psalm texture, not merged with Ps 115's own rows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Opening the row at 135:14 instead, to fold in Yahweh's compassion as a foil to the idols' impotence, was considered; kept separate because 135:14's two verbs (oshb:Ps.135.14: יָדִ֣ין, יִתְנֶחָֽם) are prefix-conjugation forms belonging with 135:13 in a distinct hinge couplet, not the suffix-conjugation forms of the historical recital (135:8, 135:10) -- and 135:14 does not yet reach the idols' inertness that 135:15 introduces as a fresh topic either way.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 149 opens under the hallelu-Yah frame (opener device, psalm_device_inventory.json verse-initial list) — הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ (oshb:Ps.149.1) — with “Praise Yahweh! The unit runs through the causal grounding clause כִּֽי רוֹצֶ֣ה יְהוָ֣ה (oshb:Ps.149.4), “For Yahweh takes pleasure in his people. He crowns the humble with salvation” (web:Ps.149.4), which closes the reason for praise. At web:Ps.149.5 the same prefix-conjugation mood continues on a changed setting — the saints on their beds rather than the dancing assembly of web:Ps.149.3 — and carries the sword theme of web:Ps.149.6, unheralded in 149:1-4; the seam is a discourse turn in setting, not a formal disjunctive marker, since the mood itself runs unbroken from web:Ps.149.2 through web:Ps.149.5.
